05-01.script:
The first of May is a day of maypoles and spring flowers, and a day to honour working people everywhere. It remembers the workers of Chicago who went on strike in 1886, demanding a working day of eight hours.

On this day in 1851, Queen Victoria opened the Great Exhibition in London, inside an enormous glittering hall of iron and glass called the Crystal Palace. Six million visitors came to marvel at inventions from around the world.

In 1931, the Empire State Building opened in New York, the tallest building on Earth. President Hoover pressed a button in Washington to switch on its lights.

In 1941, a young director named Orson Welles released Citizen Kane, a film that many still call the greatest ever made.

In 1960, the Bombay State was divided, and two new states were born: Maharashtra and Gujarat. Both celebrate today.

And in 1964, at Dartmouth College, two professors ran the first program written in BASIC, a simple language meant to let everyone, not just experts, talk to a computer.

05-02.script:
On the second of May in 1519, in a small château in the Loire valley of France, Leonardo da Vinci died. Legend says the king of France was at his side.

In 1611, a new English translation of the Bible was published, commissioned by King James. Its words, let there be light, and the salt of the earth, still live in the English language.

In 1670, King Charles the Second gave a group of merchants a charter to trade in furs around Hudson Bay. The Hudson's Bay Company is still in business today.

In 1808, the people of Madrid rose up against Napoleon's soldiers. The painter Goya would capture the terrible revenge that followed. Madrid remembers the day as Dos de Mayo.

In 1933, a Scottish newspaper reported a strange creature seen in Loch Ness, and the legend of Nessie began.

And in 1952, a de Havilland Comet took off from London for Johannesburg, the first jet airliner ever to carry paying passengers.

05-03.script:
On the third of May in 1791, the parliament of Poland and Lithuania adopted a written constitution, one of the first in the world, after the American one. Poles still celebrate it today, even though their country was soon carved up by its neighbours.

In 1494, on his second voyage, Christopher Columbus sighted the green mountains of Jamaica.

In 1913, in Bombay, audiences watched India's first full-length feature film, Raja Harishchandra, made by Dadasaheb Phalke. Because no actress would take the part, the queen was played by a young man.

In 1915, on a battlefield in Belgium, a Canadian doctor named John McCrae wrote a poem after burying a friend. In Flanders fields the poppies blow, between the crosses, row on row. The poppy became the flower of remembrance.

In 1947, Japan's new constitution came into force, promising peace.

Today is World Press Freedom Day, honouring journalists who risk everything to tell the truth.

05-04.script:
The fourth of May has become Star Wars Day, thanks to a simple pun: May the Fourth be with you.

On this day in 1799, the British stormed the fortress of Seringapatam, and Tipu Sultan, the Tiger of Mysore, died fighting at its gates.

In 1886, in Chicago's Haymarket Square, a bomb exploded at the end of a workers' rally. The violence that followed, and the trial, made the eight-hour-day movement famous around the world.

In 1904, at a hotel in Manchester, a car salesman named Charles Rolls met an engineer named Henry Royce. The name Rolls-Royce would come to mean the very best.

On that same day in 1904, the United States took over the building of the Panama Canal.

In 1919, students in Beijing marched against the peace treaty that handed Chinese land to Japan. The May Fourth Movement awakened a new China, and its young people celebrate today.

And in 1970, at Kent State University in Ohio, soldiers fired on students protesting the Vietnam War, killing four.

05-05.script:
On the fifth of May in 1862, near the Mexican city of Puebla, a small and poorly armed Mexican army defeated the mighty French. It is remembered as Cinco de Mayo, though many forget it is not Mexico's independence day.

In 1821, on the lonely island of Saint Helena, Napoleon Bonaparte died in exile. His last words, it is said, were France, the army, Josephine.

In 1891, Tchaikovsky himself conducted on the opening night of a grand new concert hall in New York, paid for by Andrew Carnegie.

In 1961, Alan Shepard climbed into a tiny capsule called Freedom 7 and became the first American in space. His flight lasted only fifteen minutes. As he waited on the launch pad, he was heard to mutter a short prayer: please, don't let me foul up.

In Japan and Korea, today is Children's Day. Families fly bright carp-shaped streamers, wishing their children strength and happiness.

05-06.script:
On the sixth of May in 1840, a little black stamp with the young Queen Victoria's profile became valid for postage in Britain. The Penny Black was the world's first adhesive postage stamp, and for a single penny a letter could go anywhere in the country.

In 1889, the World's Fair opened in Paris, its gateway a new iron tower so tall that people came from everywhere just to stand beneath it.

In 1937, the giant German airship Hindenburg burst into flames as it came in to land in New Jersey. A radio reporter cried out: oh, the humanity!

In 1954, on a cinder track in Oxford, a young medical student named Roger Bannister ran a mile in three minutes and fifty-nine point four seconds, the first person ever to run it in under four minutes. Experts had said it was impossible.

And in 1994, Queen Elizabeth and President Mitterrand opened the Channel Tunnel, linking Britain and France beneath the sea for the first time since the Ice Age.

05-07.script:
On the seventh of May in 1824, in Vienna, Beethoven's Ninth Symphony was performed for the first time. Beethoven, completely deaf, stood on stage beside the conductor. When the music ended, he was still facing the orchestra, and a singer gently turned him around so he could see the audience on its feet, waving hats and handkerchiefs.

In 1840, in the Russian town of Votkinsk, Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was born. And in 1861, in Calcutta, Rabindranath Tagore was born. He would write poems, songs and stories, win the Nobel Prize, and write the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.

In 1915, off the coast of Ireland, a German submarine sank the liner Lusitania. Nearly twelve hundred people died, and America moved closer to war.

In 1945, in a schoolhouse in Reims, Germany signed its unconditional surrender. The war in Europe was over.

And in 1954, at Dien Bien Phu in Vietnam, the French garrison fell, ending France's empire in Indochina.

05-08.script:
On the eighth of May in 1945, crowds poured into the streets of London, Paris and New York. The war in Europe was over. In London, King George and Queen Elizabeth appeared on the balcony of Buckingham Palace again and again, and Winston Churchill told the cheering crowds: this is your victory.

On this day in 1886, at a pharmacy in Atlanta, a new fizzy drink was sold for the first time, for five cents a glass. It was called Coca-Cola.

In 1902, the volcano Mount Pelée exploded on the island of Martinique, destroying the town of Saint-Pierre in minutes. One of the very few survivors was a prisoner, saved by the thick walls of his cell.

In 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler reached the summit of Everest without bottled oxygen, something many doctors had said would kill them.

And in 1980, the World Health Organization declared that smallpox, a disease that had killed hundreds of millions, had been wiped from the face of the Earth.

05-09.script:
On the ninth of May in 1671, an Irish adventurer named Colonel Thomas Blood disguised himself as a clergyman, knocked out the keeper of the Jewel House in the Tower of London, and tried to steal the Crown Jewels. He flattened the crown with a mallet to hide it under his cloak. He was caught at the gate, and to everyone's astonishment, King Charles the Second pardoned him.

In 1901, the first Parliament of a new nation, Australia, opened in Melbourne. And on this same day in 1927, a new Parliament House was opened in the purpose-built capital, Canberra.

In 1945, the war in Europe ended for the Soviet Union, a day after the West, because of the time the surrender was signed. Russia marks Victory Day with grand parades.

In 1950, the French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed that France and Germany share their coal and steel, so that war between them would become impossible. That idea grew into the European Union, which celebrates Europe Day today.

And in 1960, America approved the first birth control pill.

05-10.script:
On the tenth of May in 1857, at the army town of Meerut, Indian soldiers rose up against their British officers. That night they rode for Delhi, and declared the old Mughal emperor their leader. The great rebellion of 1857 had begun, and India's long struggle for freedom with it.

In 1752, near Paris, a French scientist followed Benjamin Franklin's suggestion, raised a tall iron rod during a thunderstorm, and drew sparks from it, proving that lightning is electricity.

In 1869, at Promontory Summit in Utah, a golden spike was tapped into place, joining two railways from east and west. America could now be crossed by train.

In 1933, students in Berlin and other cities burned tens of thousands of books by authors the Nazis disliked.

In 1940, Germany invaded the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg, and that same evening Winston Churchill became Prime Minister of Britain.

And in 1994, in Pretoria, Nelson Mandela was sworn in as President of South Africa. Never, never and never again, he said.

05-11.script:
On the eleventh of May in 1998, in the desert of Rajasthan at Pokhran, the ground shook as India tested nuclear devices. The same day, an Indian-built aircraft, the Hansa-3, flew for the first time. India celebrates National Technology Day in their memory.

In 1812, in the lobby of the House of Commons, a man with a grievance shot the Prime Minister, Spencer Perceval. He is the only British Prime Minister ever assassinated.

In 1904, in Catalonia, Salvador Dalí was born, the painter of melting clocks and dreamlike landscapes, and of an extravagant moustache.

In 1918, in New York, Richard Feynman was born. He would help explain how light and matter dance together, play the bongo drums, and crack safes for fun.

In 1949, Siam changed its name to Thailand, the Land of the Free.

And in 1997, IBM's Deep Blue computer beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a full match for the first time. Kasparov said he sensed a new kind of intelligence across the table.

05-12.script:
On the twelfth of May in 1820, in Florence, a baby girl was born and named after her birthplace. Florence Nightingale would walk the dark wards of a military hospital in the Crimean War with a lamp in her hand, and change nursing for ever. Nurses everywhere are honoured on her birthday.

In 1551, in Lima, the University of San Marcos was founded, the oldest university in the Americas.

In 1937, King George the Sixth was crowned in Westminster Abbey, and his coronation was the first ever shown on television.

In 1941, in Berlin, a German engineer named Konrad Zuse presented the Z3, the world's first working programmable computer.

In 1949, the Soviet Union lifted its blockade of West Berlin, after almost a year in which the city had been kept alive by aeroplanes.

And in 2022, astronomers revealed the first picture of the giant black hole at the centre of our own galaxy, a glowing ring of light around a dark shadow, twenty-seven thousand light-years away.

05-13.script:
On the thirteenth of May in 1607, three small ships came up a river in Virginia, and their passengers stepped ashore to found a settlement they named Jamestown. It would become the first lasting English colony in America.

In 1787, eleven ships of the First Fleet set sail from Portsmouth, bound for the far side of the world, to found the colony that would become Australia.

In 1917, in the Portuguese village of Fátima, three shepherd children said they had seen a vision of a lady brighter than the sun. Millions of pilgrims visit Fátima today.

In 1940, in his first speech as Prime Minister, Winston Churchill told Parliament: I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat.

In 1950, at Silverstone in England, the first Formula One world championship race was held.

And in 1981, in St Peter's Square, Pope John Paul the Second was shot as he greeted the crowds. He survived, and later visited the man who shot him in prison, and forgave him.

05-14.script:
On the fourteenth of May in 1796, in the English village of Berkeley, a country doctor named Edward Jenner scratched some fluid from a cowpox blister on a milkmaid's hand into the arm of an eight-year-old boy named James Phipps. Weeks later, the boy proved immune to smallpox. It was the world's first vaccine, and the beginning of the end for one of humanity's deadliest diseases.

In 1643, a four-year-old boy became King of France as Louis the Fourteenth. He would reign for seventy-two years, longer than any other monarch in European history.

In 1804, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out up the Missouri River with their Corps of Discovery, to find a route to the Pacific.

In 1948, in Tel Aviv, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel.

And in 1973, America launched Skylab, its first space station. It was damaged during launch, and the first crew had to fix it with a giant sunshade, like an umbrella.

05-15.script:
On the fifteenth of May in 1905, in the Nevada desert, a railway company auctioned off small plots of land beside its new track. The dusty little town that grew up there was called Las Vegas.

In 1918, American army pilots began the first regular airmail service, between Washington, Philadelphia and New York. The first pilot got lost, and landed in a field in Maryland.

In 1928, a cartoon mouse named Mickey appeared in a test screening of a short film called Plane Crazy.

In 1940, nylon stockings went on sale across America, and women queued around the block. On the same day, Richard and Maurice McDonald opened a small barbecue restaurant in San Bernardino, California.

In 1958, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 3, a flying laboratory full of scientific instruments.

And in 1963, astronaut Gordon Cooper rode Faith 7 on the last and longest Mercury mission, circling the Earth twenty-two times and even taking a nap in space.

Today is the International Day of Families. Perhaps call someone you love.

05-16.script:
On the sixteenth of May in 1960, in a laboratory in California, a physicist named Theodore Maiman flashed a bright lamp around a small ruby rod, and a thin, pure beam of red light shot out. It was the world's first laser. People called it a solution looking for a problem. Today lasers read our barcodes, carry our internet and heal our eyes. The world celebrates the International Day of Light on this date.

In 1770, in the chapel at Versailles, a fourteen-year-old Austrian archduchess named Marie Antoinette married the future King Louis the Sixteenth of France.

In 1929, at a small dinner in a Hollywood hotel, the first Academy Awards were handed out. The whole ceremony took about fifteen minutes.

In 1943, British bombers dropped bouncing bombs on the great dams of Germany's Ruhr valley, in the daring Dambusters raid.

And in 1975, a Japanese mountaineer named Junko Tabei became the first woman to stand on the summit of Mount Everest, just days after surviving an avalanche. On the same day, Sikkim became a state of India.

05-17.script:
On the seventeenth of May, Norway celebrates its constitution, signed at Eidsvoll in 1814. Unlike many national days, it is a day not of soldiers but of children, who march through the streets with flags, bands and ice cream.

In 1792, under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street, twenty-four stockbrokers signed a short agreement on how they would trade. It was the beginning of the New York Stock Exchange.

In 1865, twenty countries founded the International Telegraph Union, so that messages could flow across borders. It is the oldest agency of the United Nations, and the world marks World Telecommunication Day today.

In 1902, a Greek archaeologist examining bronze lumps from an ancient shipwreck noticed a gear wheel. The Antikythera mechanism turned out to be a two-thousand-year-old computer for predicting the movements of the heavens.

And in 1954, the United States Supreme Court ruled in Brown versus Board of Education that separate schools for Black and white children were unequal, and unconstitutional.

05-18.script:
On the eighteenth of May in 1048, in Persia, Omar Khayyam was born, a mathematician, an astronomer, and a poet whose verses about wine, roses and the passing of time are still read all over the world.

In 1804, Napoleon Bonaparte was proclaimed Emperor of the French. Months later, he would place the crown on his own head.

In 1910, the Earth passed through the tail of Halley's Comet. Some people were so frightened of poison gas that they bought comet pills and sealed their windows. Nothing happened at all.

In 1974, in the Rajasthan desert at Pokhran, India tested its first nuclear device. The message that it had worked was a quiet code: the Buddha is smiling.

And at 8:32 on a Sunday morning in 1980, Mount St Helens in Washington State exploded. The whole north side of the mountain slid away, and a cloud of ash rose twenty-four kilometres into the sky. The mountain lost four hundred metres of its height in minutes.

Today is International Museum Day. Perhaps visit one, and travel through time.

Napoleon is proclaimed Emperor of the French.

The Earth passes through the tail of Halley's Comet, causing panic and "comet pills".
The Tennessee Valley Authority is created.
Allied troops capture Monte Cassino.
Jacqueline Cochran becomes the first woman to fly faster than sound.
Apollo 10 is launched for a dress rehearsal of the Moon landing.
India tests its first nuclear device, codenamed Smiling Buddha.
Mount St Helens erupts in Washington State.
The Gwangju Uprising begins in South Korea.
Helen Sharman becomes the first Briton in space.
The U.S. government sues Microsoft.

births.text: Omar Khayyam, Persian poet and mathematician
Nicholas II, last Tsar of Russia
H. D. Deve Gowda, Prime Minister of India

International Museum Day was created in 1977.

names: Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day (Turkey)
05-19.script:
On the nineteenth of May in 1536, on Tower Green, Anne Boleyn, the second wife of Henry the Eighth, knelt before a swordsman brought specially from Calais. Her daughter, Elizabeth, would one day become England's greatest queen.

In 1780, the sky over New England went dark in the middle of the day. Chickens went to roost, candles were lit at noon, and some people believed the Day of Judgment had come. Scientists now think smoke from great forest fires to the north had blotted out the Sun.

In 1890, in a village in Vietnam, a boy was born who would become Ho Chi Minh. And in 1925, in Omaha, Malcolm Little was born. The world would know him as Malcolm X.

In 1919, Mustafa Kemal landed at Samsun on the Black Sea coast and began the struggle that would create modern Turkey. Turks celebrate the day as a festival of youth and sport.

And in 1962, at a birthday party in Madison Square Garden, Marilyn Monroe, in a glittering dress, sang a breathy Happy Birthday, Mr. President, to John F. Kennedy.

events.text: Anne Boleyn is executed.
New England's Dark Day turns noon into night.
Napoleon creates the Légion d'honneur.
Oscar Wilde is released from prison.
The Simplon Tunnel beneath the Alps is officially opened.
Mustafa Kemal lands at Samsun, beginning the Turkish War of Independence.
The U.S. Emergency Quota Act limits immigration.
Ho Chi Minh founds the Viet Minh.
Marilyn Monroe sings "Happy Birthday, Mr. President" to John F. Kennedy.
The Soviet Union launches Mars 2.
Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis dies.

births.text: Malcolm X, American civil rights leader

facts.text: On New England's Dark Day in 1780, candles were lit at noon, probably because of smoke from distant forest fires.
Ruskin Bond, born today, has written hundreds of stories, poems and essays, many set in the Himalayan foothills.

05-20.script:
On the twentieth of May in 1498, after ten months at sea, the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama dropped anchor near Calicut on the coast of India. He was the first European to sail all the way from Europe to India, and the spice trade of the world would never be the same.

In 1873, a tailor named Jacob Davis and a merchant named Levi Strauss received a patent for work trousers strengthened with copper rivets. Blue jeans were born.

In 1875, seventeen nations signed the Metre Convention in Paris, agreeing to share the same measures of length and weight. Scientists celebrate World Metrology Day today.

In 1927, a young pilot named Charles Lindbergh took off from a muddy field in New York, alone, in a small silver plane called the Spirit of St. Louis. He was heading for Paris.

Five years later, on this very same date in 1932, Amelia Earhart took off from Newfoundland to become the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.

And today is World Bee Day, a day to thank the small, busy creatures that pollinate so much of the food we eat.

events.text: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut, India.
Shakespeare's Sonnets are first published.
The Marquis de Lafayette dies in Paris.
President Lincoln signs the Homestead Act.
Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patent riveted blue jeans.
The Metre Convention is signed in Paris.
Thomas Edison's Kinetoscope is first shown to the public.
Cuba gains independence from the United States.
Norman Rockwell's first cover appears on The Saturday Evening Post.
Charles Lindbergh takes off on the first solo non-stop flight across the Atlantic.
Amelia Earhart sets off on the first solo transatlantic flight by a woman.
German paratroopers invade Crete.
Chiang Kai-shek is inaugurated as President of the Republic of China.
East Timor becomes independent.

facts.text: World Bee Day is held on the birthday of Anton Janša, a Slovenian pioneer of modern beekeeping.
World Metrology Day marks the signing of the Metre Convention in 1875.

05-21.script:
On the night of the twenty-first of May in 1927, thirty-three and a half hours after leaving New York, Charles Lindbergh brought his little plane down at Le Bourget airfield outside Paris. A hundred thousand people rushed across the field to greet him. He had flown the Atlantic alone, without stopping, the first person ever to do so.

Five years later, on the same day in 1932, Amelia Earhart landed in a pasture in Northern Ireland, and asked a surprised farmhand where she was. She had made it, too.

In 1881, in Washington, a nurse named Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross.

In 1904, representatives of seven countries met in Paris to found FIFA, which would one day organise the World Cup.

And in 1991, at Sriperumbudur in Tamil Nadu, former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi was killed by a suicide bomber while campaigning. India observes Anti-Terrorism Day in his memory.

Today is also International Tea Day. A good day to share a cup.

events.text: Portuguese sailors discover the island of Saint Helena.
French troops enter Paris, beginning the "Bloody Week" that ends the Commune.
Clara Barton founds the American Red Cross.
The Manchester Ship Canal is officially opened.
FIFA is founded in Paris.
Charles Lindbergh lands in Paris after flying the Atlantic alone.
Amelia Earhart lands in Northern Ireland, completing her solo transatlantic flight.
A man attacks Michelangelo's Pietà with a hammer in St Peter's Basilica.
The Empire Strikes Back is released.
Former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi is assassinated.
Ethiopian dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam flees the country.

births.text: Andrei Sakharov, Soviet physicist and Nobel Peace laureate

facts.text: Lindbergh flew 33 and a half hours alone from New York to Paris.

05-22.script:
On the twenty-second of May in 1849, a lawyer from Illinois named Abraham Lincoln received a patent for a device to lift boats over sandbars. He is still the only American president ever to hold a patent.

In 1906, the Wright brothers were at last granted their patent for a flying machine.

In 1843, about a thousand pioneers set out from Missouri in covered wagons on the long Oregon Trail, the start of the Great Emigration to the West.

In 1960, the strongest earthquake ever recorded struck Valdivia in Chile. Its tsunami crossed the whole Pacific Ocean and reached Hawaii and Japan.

In 1972, the island of Ceylon became a republic and took a new name: Sri Lanka, the resplendent land.

And in 1980, a hungry yellow circle chasing ghosts through a maze appeared in Japanese arcades. Pac-Man would become one of the most famous video games of all time.

Today is the International Day for Biological Diversity, celebrating the astonishing variety of life on Earth.

events.text: The First Battle of St Albans opens the Wars of the Roses.
About a thousand pioneers set out on the Oregon Trail.
Abraham Lincoln receives a patent for a device to lift boats over sandbars.
Senator Charles Sumner is beaten with a cane in the U.S. Senate.
The Wright brothers are granted a patent for their flying machine.
Germany and Italy sign the Pact of Steel.
The Valdivia earthquake in Chile, the strongest ever recorded, strikes.
Ceylon becomes the Republic of Sri Lanka.
Richard Nixon visits Moscow, the first U.S. president to do so.
Pac-Man is released in Japan.
North and South Yemen unite.
Johnny Carson hosts his final Tonight Show.

births.text: Ram Mohan Roy, Indian social reformer
Arthur Conan Doyle, Scottish author (Sherlock Holmes)

facts.text: Abraham Lincoln is the only U.S. president to have held a patent.
The 1960 Valdivia earthquake, magnitude 9.5, is the strongest ever recorded.

05-23.script:
On the twenty-third of May in 1430, Joan of Arc was captured by Burgundian soldiers at Compiègne, pulled from her horse as she guarded the rear of her retreating troops. A year later, she would be burned at the stake.

In 1618, in Prague, angry Protestant nobles threw two royal officials and their secretary out of a high castle window. All three survived, landing, it is said, on a pile of dung. The Defenestration of Prague started the Thirty Years' War.

In 1707, in Sweden, Carl Linnaeus was born. He gave every plant and animal a two-part Latin name, like Homo sapiens for us, and brought order to the living world.

In 1785, Benjamin Franklin, tired of switching between two pairs of glasses, wrote to a friend about his invention: lenses cut in half, near and far. We call them bifocals.

And in 1934, in Louisiana, the outlaws Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow drove into an ambush, and their wild crime spree came to an end.

events.text: Joan of Arc is captured at Compiègne.
The Defenestration of Prague starts the Thirty Years' War.
Benjamin Franklin describes his invention of bifocals.
Cyrill Demian patents the accordion in Vienna.
The North-West Mounted Police, today's Mounties, is created.
Playwright Henrik Ibsen dies.
The New York Public Library is dedicated.
Bonnie and Clyde are killed in an ambush.
Heinrich Himmler dies in British custody.
West Germany is founded.
Tibet and China sign the Seventeen Point Agreement.
Italian anti-mafia judge Giovanni Falcone is murdered.
The Java programming language is released.

facts.text: Carl Linnaeus, born today, gave living things two-part Latin names, like Homo sapiens.

05-24.script:
On the twenty-fourth of May in 1543, in the Polish town of Frombork, the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus lay dying. Legend says that, on his last day, a copy of his great book arrived from the printer, the book that moved the Earth from the centre of the universe, and was placed in his hands.

In 1844, in the Capitol in Washington, Samuel Morse tapped out a message on his telegraph to Baltimore, sixty kilometres away. It came from the Bible: What hath God wrought.

In 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge opened across New York's East River, the longest suspension bridge in the world. A week later, a rumour that it was about to collapse caused a deadly stampede. To prove its strength, the circus showman P. T. Barnum later led twenty-one elephants across it.

In 1819, Princess Victoria was born. She would become queen at eighteen and reign for sixty-three years.

And in 1941, in the North Atlantic, the German battleship Bismarck sank the great British warship Hood. Of more than fourteen hundred men aboard, only three survived.

events.text: Copernicus dies, said to have just received his printed book.
John Wesley's heart is "strangely warmed", the beginning of Methodism.
The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad begins the first scheduled passenger service in the U.S.
Samuel Morse sends "What hath God wrought" by telegraph.
The Brooklyn Bridge opens.
The first night game in major league baseball is played.
The Bismarck sinks HMS Hood.
The first Eurovision Song Contest is held, in Switzerland.
Eritrea becomes independent.
Israel withdraws from southern Lebanon.

births.text: William Whewell, English scientist who coined the word "scientist"

facts.text: William Whewell, born today, coined the word "scientist".
P. T. Barnum led 21 elephants across the Brooklyn Bridge to prove it was safe.

05-25.script:
On the twenty-fifth of May in 1810, in Buenos Aires, crowds gathered in the rain outside the town council, and the first government of an independent Argentina was formed. Argentines still celebrate the May Revolution.

In 1935, at a track meet in Michigan, a young athlete named Jesse Owens set three world records and equalled a fourth, all within forty-five minutes.

In 1961, President Kennedy stood before Congress and asked America to land a man on the Moon and return him safely to the Earth before the decade was out. Eight years later, it was done.

In 1963, leaders of thirty-two independent African nations met in Addis Ababa and founded the Organisation of African Unity. Africa Day celebrates that dream of a united continent.

And in 1977, a film opened in just a few dozen cinemas, about a farm boy, a princess, a smuggler and a galaxy far, far away. Star Wars would change the movies for ever.

Today is also Towel Day, when fans of Douglas Adams carry a towel, the most useful thing an interstellar hitchhiker can have.

events.text: The U.S. Constitutional Convention opens in Philadelphia.
The May Revolution begins Argentina's independence.
Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore opens in London.
Oscar Wilde is convicted and sentenced to two years' hard labour.
Jesse Owens sets three world records in 45 minutes.
President Kennedy announces the goal of landing a man on the Moon.
The Organisation of African Unity is founded.
Star Wars is released.
Millions join hands across the United States in Hands Across America.
NASA's Phoenix lander touches down near the north pole of Mars.
SpaceX's Dragon becomes the first commercial spacecraft to dock with the International Space Station.

facts.text: Towel Day honours Douglas Adams; fans carry a towel, "the most useful thing an interstellar hitchhiker can have".
Africa Day marks the founding of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963.

05-26.script:
On the twenty-sixth of May in 1828, a strange teenage boy appeared in the streets of Nuremberg, holding a letter and barely able to speak. Kaspar Hauser said he had spent his whole childhood alone in a dark cell. Who he really was remains a mystery to this day.

In 1896, Charles Dow published the first Dow Jones Industrial Average, an average of the share prices of twelve companies. On the same day in Moscow, Nicholas the Second was crowned the last Tsar of Russia.

In 1897, a novel was published in London about a Transylvanian count who slept in a coffin by day. Bram Stoker's Dracula has been haunting readers ever since.

In 1940, at the French port of Dunkirk, the evacuation began. Over nine days, destroyers, ferries and hundreds of little fishing boats and pleasure craft rescued more than three hundred thousand Allied soldiers from the beaches.

And in 1951, in Los Angeles, Sally Ride was born. In 1983, she became the first American woman in space.

events.text: The mysterious Kaspar Hauser appears in Nuremberg.
The U.S. Senate acquits President Andrew Johnson by one vote.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average is first published.
Nicholas II is crowned Tsar of Russia.
Bram Stoker's Dracula is published.
Georgia declares independence.
The first 24 Hours of Le Mans race is run.
The last Ford Model T rolls off the production line, after more than 15 million were made.
The evacuation of Dunkirk begins.
Guyana gains independence from Britain.
Apollo 10 returns to Earth after its Moon-landing dress rehearsal.
Nixon and Brezhnev sign the SALT I treaty.

births.text: Sally Ride, first American woman in space

facts.text: Sally Ride, born today, became the first American woman in space in 1983.

05-27.script:
On the twenty-seventh of May in 1703, on marshy islands where the River Neva meets the sea, Tsar Peter the Great founded a new city, built in stone to be his window on Europe. He named it Saint Petersburg.

In 1905, in the Tsushima Strait between Korea and Japan, the Japanese navy destroyed a Russian fleet that had sailed halfway around the world to meet it. For the first time in modern history, an Asian power had defeated a European one at sea.

In 1919, a U.S. Navy flying boat called NC-4 landed in Lisbon, completing the first flight across the Atlantic, in several hops.

In 1937, the Golden Gate Bridge opened in San Francisco. On the first day, two hundred thousand people walked across it.

In 1941, after a long chase across the Atlantic, the British navy sank the German battleship Bismarck.

And in 1964, India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, died in Delhi. The man who had told India at midnight of its tryst with destiny was gone.

events.text: Peter the Great founds Saint Petersburg.
Japan destroys the Russian fleet at the Battle of Tsushima.
The NC-4 flying boat completes the first flight across the Atlantic.
The Chrysler Building opens in New York.
Auguste Piccard becomes the first person to reach the stratosphere, in a balloon.
The Chicago World's Fair opens.
The Golden Gate Bridge opens.
The British navy sinks the battleship Bismarck.
Jawaharlal Nehru dies.
Australians vote overwhelmingly to include Aboriginal people in the national census.
Slobodan Milošević is indicted for war crimes.

facts.text: The Golden Gate Bridge's colour is called "International Orange".
Peter the Great made Saint Petersburg the capital of Russia in 1712.

05-28.script:
On the twenty-eighth of May in 585 BC, the Lydians and the Medes were fighting a fierce battle in what is now Turkey when the Sun suddenly went dark. A total eclipse. Both armies were so frightened that they laid down their weapons and made peace. It is said the philosopher Thales had predicted it.

In 1588, the great Spanish Armada of some hundred and thirty ships set sail from Lisbon to invade England.

In 1934, in a farmhouse in Ontario, five identical baby girls were born, the Dionne quintuplets, the first quintuplets known to survive infancy.

In 1959, two small monkeys named Able and Baker rode a rocket into space and came back alive, the first primates to return safely.

And in 1987, a nineteen-year-old West German pilot named Mathias Rust flew a small plane through Soviet air defences and landed it right beside Red Square in Moscow. Generals lost their jobs; Rust became a legend.

Azerbaijan and Armenia both celebrate today the founding of their first republics in 1918.

events.text: The Spanish Armada sets sail from Lisbon.
President Andrew Jackson signs the Indian Removal Act.
John Muir founds the Sierra Club.
Azerbaijan and Armenia declare independence.
The Dionne quintuplets are born in Canada.
Volkswagen is founded.
Belgium surrenders to Germany.
Monkeys Able and Baker return safely from space.
Peter Benenson's article "The Forgotten Prisoners" launches Amnesty International.
Mathias Rust lands a small plane near Red Square in Moscow.
Pakistan carries out its first nuclear tests.
Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper is unveiled after 22 years of restoration.

births.text: N. T. Rama Rao, Indian actor and Chief Minister

facts.text: An eclipse said to have been predicted by Thales stopped a battle between the Lydians and Medes in 585 BC.

05-29.script:
On the morning of the twenty-ninth of May in 1953, a New Zealand beekeeper named Edmund Hillary and a Sherpa named Tenzing Norgay climbed the last snowy ridge and stood on the summit of Mount Everest, the highest place on Earth. Tenzing left some sweets in the snow as an offering. Hillary took a photograph of his friend, flags fluttering from his ice axe.

Five hundred years earlier, in 1453, the walls of Constantinople fell to the Ottoman army of Sultan Mehmed the Second, and the Byzantine Empire, the last of Rome, came to an end.

In 1660, on his thirtieth birthday, Charles the Second rode into London to reclaim his throne. People wore oak leaves to remember how he had once hidden in an oak tree to escape his enemies.

In 1913, in Paris, Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring was so strange and wild that the audience broke into a riot.

And in 1919, during a solar eclipse, Arthur Eddington photographed stars near the Sun and found their light was bent, just as Einstein had predicted. Einstein became famous overnight.

events.text: Constantinople falls to the Ottoman Empire.
Charles II returns to London on his birthday, restoring the monarchy.
Rhode Island becomes the last of the thirteen colonies to ratify the Constitution.
Wisconsin becomes the 30th U.S. state.
Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring causes a riot at its premiere.
Arthur Eddington's eclipse photographs confirm Einstein's theory of relativity.
Bing Crosby records "White Christmas".
The first UN peacekeeping mission is created, in the Middle East.
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reach the summit of Everest.
Boris Yeltsin is elected leader of the Russian republic.
Space Shuttle Discovery makes the first docking with the International Space Station.

births.text: John F. Kennedy, 35th President of the United States
Peter Higgs, British physicist (the Higgs boson)

facts.text: Oak Apple Day remembers Charles II hiding in an oak tree after the Battle of Worcester.
Tenzing Norgay left sweets in the snow on Everest's summit as an offering.

05-30.script:
On the thirtieth of May in 1431, in the marketplace at Rouen, Joan of Arc, just nineteen years old, was burned at the stake. Twenty-five years later, a court declared her innocent, and in 1920 she was made a saint.

In 1826, in Calcutta, a small newspaper appeared called Udant Martand, the Rising Sun. It was the first newspaper in Hindi, and India celebrates Hindi Journalism Day today.

In 1868, Americans laid flowers on the graves of soldiers who had died in the Civil War, on the first Decoration Day, which grew into Memorial Day.

In 1911, forty cars lined up for the first Indianapolis 500 race. And in 1922, the Lincoln Memorial was dedicated in Washington, with the great marble president gazing out over the Reflecting Pool.

In 1967, the eastern region of Nigeria declared itself the independent Republic of Biafra, beginning a tragic civil war.

And in 1987, Goa, with its beaches, churches and spice gardens, became the twenty-fifth state of India.

events.text: Joan of Arc is burned at the stake in Rouen.
Udant Martand, the first Hindi newspaper, is published in Calcutta.
The Kansas–Nebraska Act becomes law.
The first Decoration Day, later Memorial Day, is observed.
The first Indianapolis 500 race is held.
The Lincoln Memorial is dedicated.
NASA launches Surveyor 1 towards the Moon.
Biafra declares independence from Nigeria.
NASA launches Mariner 9, which will become the first spacecraft to orbit Mars.
The European Space Agency is founded.
Goa becomes a state of India.

births.text: Mel Blanc, American voice actor (Bugs Bunny)
Alexei Leonov, first person to walk in space

facts.text: Hindi Journalism Day marks the first issue of Udant Martand, published in Calcutta in 1826.
Mel Blanc, born today, was the voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig.

05-31.script:
On the thirty-first of May in 1725, in a village in Maharashtra, a girl named Ahilyabai was born. She would become queen of Indore, and rule with such wisdom and kindness that temples, wells and rest-houses she built still stand all across India.

In 1859, the great clock in the tower of the Palace of Westminster began to keep time. Its biggest bell, Big Ben, rang out for the first time weeks later.

In 1889, after days of heavy rain, an old dam above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, burst. A wall of water swept through the town.

In 1911, in Belfast, the hull of the Titanic slid down the slipway into the water for the first time, as a hundred thousand people watched.

In 1916, the British and German fleets met in the North Sea at Jutland, the greatest sea battle of the First World War.

And in 1910 and 1961, on this same date, South Africa was first united as one country, then declared a republic.

Today the world marks World No Tobacco Day.

events.text: The first U.S. copyright law is signed.
The great clock at Westminster, home of Big Ben, begins keeping time.
New York's first Madison Square Garden opens under that name.
The Johnstown Flood kills more than 2,200 people.
The Treaty of Vereeniging ends the Second Boer War.
The Union of South Africa is formed.
The Titanic is launched in Belfast.
The Battle of Jutland is fought in the North Sea.
South Africa becomes a republic.
Adolf Eichmann is executed in Israel.
"Deep Throat", the Watergate source, is revealed to be Mark Felt.

births.text: Clint Eastwood, American actor and director

facts.text: Big Ben is the name of the great bell; the tower is called the Elizabeth Tower.
World No Tobacco Day was created by the World Health Organization in 1987.
